caption:
How to track wedding RSVPs: four methods, compared honestly. Paper, a reply page, group chats and QR codes each have a catch, and this video names every one so you can pick a main path and a fallback.
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment:
The four RSVP methods, and the catch for each:
1. Paper reply card: formal, no phone needed. Catch: replies come by mail and you type each one in.
2. Reply page on the web: answers land in one place. Catch: guests need a phone and a signal, and a page can't make anyone answer.
3. Group chat or texts: fast and familiar. Catch: answers scatter, and a thumbs-up isn't an RSVP.
4. QR code on printed paper: no web address to type. Catch: label it and print the address underneath.
Pick one main path plus a fallback, and count back from your caterer's date to set the reply-by date.
Sources: Pew Research Center (2025), The Knot survey via The New York Times (2026), Emily Post Institute, Business Insider (2021), Joy (2025).
Norah is AI-generated. Screens shown are real Wedillybird screens (demo data).

claims_review.notes: No competitor compared. Product appears once (S04 over two beats, about 8 s): one personal link per guest, nothing to install; honest limits spoken (needs phone and signal; a page cannot make anyone answer). 'One etiquette specialist' is Anne Chertoff, named on screen (T36 is medium: single expert). The 49% Knot QR figure is deliberately not used (T37 medium); 59% is the NYT-reported 2026 figure (medium-high). Only the Pew WhatsApp age row (20% at 65+) is used, as advice context for group chats, never as a product channel; the 78% smartphone row is left to another video. No QR image on screen. Reply-by guidance follows T30 (sources vary: Knot four to two weeks, Emily Post two to three weeks), so no single deadline is stated as the rule.
